Henry notices that the prophet needed no waking this time, nor even a summons to look about him, but turns and lifts up his eyes of his own accord — a gain, he says, that good men sometimes get by their infirmities, which make them more careful and circumspect afterwards. Gill puts the turning in relation to what went before, the prophet having had a full understanding of the candlestick and the olive branches and now looking another way. Ellicott would render it rather that he again lifted up his eyes, and thinks the form of the vision suggested by the roll shown to an earlier prophet, written within and without; Henry makes the same comparison and adds that as the command of the law is in writing, for certainty and perpetuity, so is its curse, which writes bitter things against the sinner. Ellicott also records that the Septuagint, dropping the last letter of the word for scroll, rendered it a sickle instead.

Whether the chapter contains one vision or two divides Clarke from Keil and Delitzsch. Clarke heads them separately, the flying roll with its explanation and then the ephah with the woman sitting on it. Keil and Delitzsch argue that the two figures are so closely connected as to be taken as one vision, and answer the obvious objection directly: the pause between the two views, in which the ecstatic elevation and the interpreting angel both leave the prophet, furnishes no sufficient reason for assuming two different visions.

The dimensions given to the roll draw out Ellicott's most striking observation. They are, he notes, the dimensions of the holy place of the tabernacle and of the porch of the temple, so that if the measurement is symbolic it indicates that the measure of the sanctuary is the measure of sin: the sinner must not say that he is no worse than his neighbour, but must measure his conduct by the standard that bids him be holy because God is holy. Clarke takes the roll instead as an allusion to the great rolls on which the Pentateuch is written,. On the two sins named, Clarke observes that the roll was written on front and back and that stealing and swearing stand as two general heads, the one comprising sins against men and the other sins against God.

Whose crimes are recorded is genuinely disputed. Clarke reports both opinions, that they are the crimes of the Jews and that they are the crimes of the Chaldeans, and adopts the second, identifying the house that the curse enters as Babylon, the city of a king who was a public plunderer and a glaring idolater. Ellicott renders the phrase not the whole earth but the whole land, meaning Israel. Wesley leaves it open between the land of Judea and all the world, wherever these sins are found. Gill takes the curse for the law of Moses, so called because curses are written in it, and reports an interpreter who referred the passage to the times of Antiochus. Calvin dismisses the field with unusual sharpness, saying that interpreters have touched neither heaven nor earth in explaining this prophecy because they have not regarded the design of the Holy Spirit, and rejecting in particular the view that the volume means the false and perverted glosses by which the purity of doctrine had been corrupted; his own account is that whatever evils the Jews suffered proceeded from the righteous judgment of God. Ellicott closes with a parallel from Herodotus, of a man who asked the oracle whether he might perjure himself to keep money left on trust with him; Wesley says the curse will stick close to the offender and his house like the leprosy that clung to Gehazi.

Henry contrasts this vision with the one before, which was plain and easy, whereas here are things dark and hard to be understood; and he offers a reason for the obscurity, quoting an earlier expositor by name. Some think the scope of the vision is to foretell the final destruction of the Jewish church and nation and the dispersion of the people once they had filled up the measure of their iniquities; and it is therefore set out deliberately in obscure figures, lest a plain denunciation of the second overthrow of temple and state should discourage them from going forward with the present restoration of both. Wesley repeats the same explanation in his own words. Gill and Ellicott both mark the movement of the interpreting angel at the opening, Ellicott taking his going forth to mean that he emerges from the region of the invisible into that of the visible.

What the ephah and the woman signify divides them. Clarke makes the woman the impiety of the Jewish nation, the mass of its iniquity, and the talent of lead the wrath of God bending down a culprit nation under the measure of its sins. Wesley says the same briefly, that the woman represents the wickedness of the Jews and that the lead shut her up to suffer the punishment of all her sins. Ellicott reads the figure as a symbol of the sinners named in the previous vision, and explains the comparison: as the separate grains are all gathered together in an ephah, so will the individual sinners be gathered; he notes too that the Septuagint, by the change of a single letter, read iniquity where our text has resemblance. Gill applies the whole to the Roman antichrist, whose title is his Holiness but whose true and proper name, he says, is wickedness.

Gill supplies the weights with unusual care, reckoning a talent at three thousand shekels and reporting the estimates in English measure at a hundred and twenty-five pounds or, on a more exact computation, a hundred and thirteen pounds and a fraction of Troy weight, before turning to the different reckoning of a Babylonish talent. Wesley keeps to the picture, a piece of lead as large as the mouth of the ephah, brought to cover it. Keil and Delitzsch set the sequence out plainly without interpretation, the ephah going forth, wickedness cast in, and the weight of lead thrown on the mouth.

On the two women who carry it away Clarke allegorises and Ellicott declines to. Clarke makes them the desperate unbelief of the Jews in rejecting the Messiah and the corruption of manners that followed,. Ellicott says we need not enter into the minute details, which are probably introduced merely to give the picture greater distinctness, though he allows the wings seem filled with wind to carry the burden more easily, and suggests the prophet may have borrowed his imagery from grotesque figures he had seen in Babylon. Gill insists that this is not a new vision but a continuation of the former, as the reappearing ephah shows, where Ellicott calls it the third scene. Of the destination they divide again: Gill takes Shinar for the province of Babylon and the carrying thither as denoting the cause of the captivity, the measure of sins filled up. Clarke reads Shinar as Babylon and Babylon in turn as Rome, so that the house built for the imprisoned woman signifies a long captivity under the Romans — a house which, he adds, remains to this day, the woman still in the ephah, set on her own base as a distinct nation, with the lead of God's displeasure still on the top. Wesley agrees, taking the base to mean that they are settled upon the lees of their own unbelief.
